sources: NPS Observing Bald Eagles in Cuyahoga Valley

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; spring offers the highest water flow over the falls
trails.trailTip: The overlook platforms keep you back from the gorge edge — stay on the platform and marked trail rather than scrambling down toward the falls, since the shale slopes are unstable and slick when wet.
trails.didYouKnow: Brandywine Falls drops 65 feet, making it the tallest waterfall in the park.

trails.trailTip: The path winds beneath overhangs and past narrow rock crevices — sturdy shoes help on the uneven, sometimes damp sandstone underfoot.
trails.didYouKnow: The sandstone ledges were quarried in the 1800s, and old chisel marks are still visible on some of the rock faces along the trail.

trails.estimatedTime: Varies by segment; full length is a multi-hour or multi-day trip
trails.bestSeason: Year-round; flattest, most accessible trail in the park
trails.trailTip: The crushed-limestone surface is flat and wheelchair- and stroller-friendly, but it's shared with cyclists — stay to the right and listen for bell signals when passing.
trails.didYouKnow: The Towpath Trail follows the original path where mules once walked to tow canal boats along the 19th-century Ohio & Erie Canal.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; spring and after rain give the strongest flow
trails.trailTip: The short spur down to the falls' base gets slick with mist and mud — wear shoes with good tread and give the ledge above the falls extra space in wet weather.
trails.didYouKnow: Blue Hen Falls is one of the park's most photographed waterfalls despite requiring only a short walk from the trailhead.

trails.trailTip: This loop combines several connector trails near Boston Mills, so carry a park trail map — junctions aren't always obvious even though the tread is well maintained.
trails.didYouKnow: This section is part of the larger 1,400-mile Buckeye Trail, which loops all the way around the state of Ohio.

trails.trailTip: Wetmore links directly into the Buckeye Trail network near Boston, so double-check trail blazes at junctions to stay on the loop you intend.
trails.didYouKnow: The Wetmore Trail passes through second-growth forest that has reclaimed what was farmland just a century ago.

trails.trailTip: The trail crosses several old farm fields now reverting to meadow — watch footing where the path narrows through brush after wet weather.
trails.didYouKnow: Remnants of old fence lines and foundation stones from former farms are still visible along parts of the Salt Run corridor.

trails.trailTip: This loop near Kendall Lake connects easily with the Ledges area — bring a map since several trails intersect nearby.
trails.didYouKnow: The Plateau Trail passes several smaller, less-visited sandstone ledge formations similar to the more famous ones on the main Ledges Trail.

animals.whereToLook: Forest edges and meadows throughout the valley
animals.viewingTip: During the fall rut, watch bucks from a distance with binoculars — a rutting buck is more on edge than usual and should never be approached or crowded for a photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Cuyahoga Valley has one of the densest deer populations of any unit in the National Park System, largely due to a lack of natural predators in the surrounding developed landscape.

animals.whereToLook: A large rookery visible from the Towpath Trail near Bath Road
animals.viewingTip: View the rookery from the marked Towpath overlook with binoculars or a spotting scope rather than approaching the nest trees, since a colony disturbed during nesting season can abandon eggs or chicks.
animals.didYouKnow: The Bath Road heronry has grown to become one of the largest great blue heron rookeries in Ohio, with dozens of nests crowded into a stand of dead trees.

animals.bestSeason: Year-round; more vocal Jan-Feb during breeding season
animals.whereToLook: Meadows and forest edges throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: If you hear howling at dusk, stay put and listen rather than trying to approach — coyotes are naturally wary of people and are best experienced by ear.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes reestablished themselves in the Cuyahoga Valley on their own over the past several decades as the region's forest cover recovered.

animals.whereToLook: The Cuyahoga River and adjacent wetlands, including near Beaver Marsh
animals.viewingTip: Watch quietly from the bank or a boardwalk with binoculars — otters are playful but skittish, and will disappear underwater quickly if you approach or make noise.
animals.didYouKnow: River otters were reintroduced to Ohio in the 1980s after being wiped out by pollution and habitat loss, and the Cuyahoga River's cleanup helped make their return here possible.

animals.bestSeason: Year-round; most active building in fall before winter
animals.whereToLook: Beaver Marsh and other wetland areas along the Towpath Trail
animals.viewingTip: Watch dams and lodges from the boardwalk with binoculars around dusk, and never approach a lodge closely — a disturbed beaver may slap its tail on the water and dive, cutting the sighting short.
animals.didYouKnow: Beaver Marsh got its name because beavers moved into a former junkyard site and, through decades of dam-building, transformed it into the wetland that exists today.

animals.whereToLook: Along the Cuyahoga River, including a long-active nest near Pinery Narrows north of Station Road Bridge
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, a stretch of the old railroad right-of-way near the Pinery Narrows nest is closed to foot traffic during the nesting season — view eagles from the open Towpath Trail or a permitted overlook with binoculars and respect any posted closure signs.
animals.didYouKnow: The same pair of bald eagles has returned to nest in the Cuyahoga Valley nearly every year since 2007, having raised more than a dozen eaglets there.

animals.whereToLook: Meadows and forest edges throughout the valley
animals.viewingTip: If you locate a den by tracks or scat nearby, view it from well back with binoculars and move on — lingering near an active den can cause a vixen to abandon it or relocate her kits.
animals.didYouKnow: Red fox kits are born blind and helpless but are already exploring outside the den entrance within about a month.

animals.whereToLook: Beaver Marsh and other quiet wetlands along the Towpath Trail
animals.viewingTip: Scan nest boxes and shoreline snags from the boardwalk with binoculars — wood ducks are easily startled off the water, so keep noise down and stay on the trail rather than pushing into the marsh edge.
animals.didYouKnow: Wood duck chicks leap from tree cavity nests up to 50 feet above ground within a day of hatching and bounce off the forest floor largely unharmed.
